summary: Fluorouracil (5-FU) is an intravenous fluoropyrimidine antimetabolite used in adenocarcinoma of the colon/rectum, breast, stomach and pancreas, usually combined with leucovorin and other agents. Patients with low or absent dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) activity are at risk of severe or fatal toxicity (mucositis, diarrhea, neutropenia, neurotoxicity). It can cause cardiotoxicity, hyperammonemic encephalopathy, acute cerebellar syndrome, severe diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome, myelosuppression and mucositis, and markedly raises INR with warfarin. Dose and schedule must be individualized by regimen; uridine triacetate is the antidote for overdose/early severe toxicity.
indications: Adenocarcinoma of the colon and rectum

moa: A nucleoside metabolic inhibitor converted to active metabolites FdUMP (inhibits thymidylate synthase, blocking dTMP/DNA synthesis), FUTP (misincorporated into RNA) and FdUTP (incorporated into DNA), interfering with DNA and RNA synthesis and causing death of rapidly growing cells.

relative: Low or absent DPD (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase) activity - severe/fatal toxicity risk
Severe myelosuppression or active serious infection
monitor: INR if on a vitamin K antagonist
Serum ammonia if altered mental status

preg: Pregnancy Category D. Based on its mechanism, fluorouracil can cause fetal harm; animal data show embryolethality and teratogenicity (cleft palate, skeletal defects). Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during and for up to 3 months after the last dose; counsel males to use contraception during and for 3 months after.
lact: It is not known whether fluorouracil or its metabolites are present in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed infant, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or to discontinue the drug.
renal: Metabolites (e.g. urea, alpha-fluoro-beta-alanine) are excreted renally; use caution and monitor for increased toxicity in renal impairment.
hepatic: Fluorouracil is largely metabolized in the liver and distributes to liver tissue; use caution and monitor in hepatic impairment.

major: Warfarin / vitamin K antagonists - clinically significant increases in coagulation parameters/INR and bleeding; monitor INR and prothrombin time closely
Brivudine/sorivudine - DPD inhibition causing life-threatening fluoropyrimidine toxicity (contraindicated combination)
moderate: CYP2C9 substrates (e.g. phenytoin) - possible increased levels via CYP2C9 inhibition
Leucovorin - enhances 5-FU activity and toxicity (used therapeutically but increases AE risk)
minor: Other myelosuppressive/cytotoxic agents - additive marrow suppression
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive GI and mucosal toxicity
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate INR/PT with warfarin; monitor coagulation closely

pearls: TOXICITY: low/absent DPD (DPYD variants) causes severe or fatal early-onset toxicity - mucositis, diarrhea, neutropenia, neurotoxicity; test before treating where possible and withhold/stop for unusually severe early toxicity
Uridine triacetate is the antidote - give within 96 hours of the end of the fluorouracil infusion for overdose or early-onset severe toxicity
Cardiotoxicity (vasospastic angina/MI) can occur, more with continuous infusion - withhold for cardiac symptoms
Markedly raises INR with warfarin (same effect seen with the prodrug capecitabine) - monitor closely
missed: Fluorouracil is administered by clinicians on a fixed protocol schedule; there is no patient self-administered make-up dose. If an infusion is delayed or interrupted, the oncology team adjusts timing per protocol - do not attempt to compensate at home.
overdose: Manifests as severe 5-FU toxicity: nausea, vomiting, severe diarrhea, GI ulceration/bleeding, profound myelosuppression and neurotoxicity. Administer uridine triacetate within 96 hours following the end of the fluorouracil infusion. Provide supportive care, monitor and treat cytopenias, fluids/electrolytes; hospitalize and consult toxicology/oncology.
